newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Politicians say Krupp-Thyssen deal inevitable.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Politicians say Krupp-Thyssen deal inevitable.

text.p: Two of Germany's oldest industry groups, Thyssen and Krupp, won support on Friday to merge their steel operations from Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt amid speculation Krupp has secured a sizeable stake in its rival.

Speaking at a coal industry conference in Gelsenkirchen, Rexrodt said a merger of the steel operations of Thyssen and Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp, which have an annual turnover of some 63 billion marks ($37 billion), was inevitable and that it would be good for the industry.
He said that talks which opened this week on a mutually acceptable deal between Krupp and Thyssen were clearly going well after Krupp suspended its hostile takeover bid.
"The goal of all efforts must be to strengthen the competitiveness of the German steel industry and to secure jobs," he said. "Germany must keep its steel base."
Speculation surfaced on Friday that Krupp might not have given up efforts to take control of its larger rival.

Banking sources said it was likely that institutional investors had secured a big chunk of Thyssen shares on behalf of Krupp and the business daily Handelsblatt said Krupp had secured 30 percent of Thyssen's capital through institutional investors.
But Krupp denied the newspaper report that it had gained control of some 30 percent of Thyssen stock.
"That is not correct. We do not have any Thyssen shares," a Krupp spokesman said, adding that Krupp's banks had not accumulated Thyssen shares on its behalf either.

Germany's BAWe securuties trading watchdog said it had not been notified of any accumulation of Thyssen stock exceeding five percent. Under German law, companies must report stakes in other corporations when they reach the five percent mark.

Krupp launched a surprise bid last week with backing from Germany's two largest banks, Deutsche Bank AG and Dresdner Bank AG, and U.S. investment house Goldman Sachs. It suspended the bid after Thyssen agreed to enter week-long negotiations on forming a joint steel company.
Banking sources said that even without a base of Thyssen shares in hand, Krupp was determined to use a fusion with Thyssen to produce a reinvigorated German steel giant.

Krupp chairman Gerhard Cromme's disregard of Germany's traditional shyness of such hostile takeovers has been sharply criticised but also won some support from those who see it as the only way to speed up needed restructuring.

"The company is determinted to bring about something new in Germany -- and it is very determined to stick by the rules," said one source close to the deal of the reports that Krupp had gained control of a large block of Thyssen shares.
A Dresdner Bank spokesman told Reuters, "We welcome Krupp's initiative to secure a merger in the steel sector. We think this is a positive move and are giving financial support."
Another source close to the deal said that Krupp had launched its bid because "Thyssen had no protection for its shares."

Thyssen, in contrast with many other traditional German companies, has few large blocks of stock owned by shareholders it could count on to help ward off such hostile takeover attempts. Insurance group Allianz AG, which owns eight percent of Thyssen's stock, has said it is considering the Krupp bid.
Krupp offered Thyssen shareholders 435 marks per share -- 25 percent more than the stock price at the time and 60 percent over the price of the shares at the end of 1996.

Thyssen, with 9.5 billion marks in steel sales, is the top producer in Germany but only number five in Europe. Krupp is smaller, with 5.2 billion in steel revenue. Together the companies would rival Europe's two largest steel makers, France's Unisor Sacilor and British Steel.

The state of North Rhine-Westphalia, home for both Krupp and Thyssen, hopes a deal could be reached to help revitalise the region, which has been hard-hit by the depressions in coal and steel, state premier Johannes Rau said on Friday.

"We must accelerate structural change," he said at the coal conference in Gelsenkirchen. Rau added he was sure that the two would find a common business solution through cooperation and described the talks as "serious".
